Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 13, verse 1:

Lesson No. 112: Explanation of Verses 1 to 18

The Surah opens with one of the fundamental issues of the Islamic worldview: that this Book has been revealed from Allah, and that the truths it contains are true and real. This matter is among the foundations of the Islamic worldview. All other beliefs and doctrines are built upon this point. The belief in Tawhid (the Oneness of Allah), the belief in resurrection after death, the benefit of righteous deeds in life, and all moral teachings depend on the fact that all these commands are from Allah, and that they came from Allah in the form of the Qur'an through Jibril (peace be upon him). Hadrat Muhammad (ﷺ) is true. This is the foundation on which the whole religion has been built.

Verse No. 1

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book.﴾ That is, these verses bear witness that this revelation is from Allah, because these verses are composed of the same letters of the alphabet. And since until today no one has been able to produce a book like this from these letters, it is proven that these are the revelation of Allah.

﴿And what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth.﴾ This is the truth; it is a pure truth in which there is no admixture of falsehood, and in which there is no doubt or hesitation. These letters of the alphabet are also evidence that it is the truth, because they are a clear proof of the Book's being from Allah. What comes from Allah is certainly the truth, and there is no room for doubt in it.

﴿But most of the people do not believe.﴾ They do not believe that this Qur'an is from Allah, nor do they accept the consequences that follow from this faith, such as the belief in Tawhid, complete obedience to Allah alone, the belief in resurrection after death, and righteous deeds accompanied by Tawhid, and the reform of the whole of life.

This is the opening of this Surah, and within it the subjects of the whole Surah have been condensed and enclosed. Indication has been given to all the topics present in it. Accordingly, the detailed discussion begins with a description of the signs of Allah's power: how the creation of this universe, its movement, and its effects and traces are based on profound wisdom, and how wondrous the universe itself is. When the universe is wondrous, its creation is wondrous, and its wisdoms are beyond comprehension, then revelation and Book are indispensable for the guidance of man, and it is also necessary that there be an everlasting life after this transient world. Moreover, the demand of this intricate power and wisdom of the universe is, as a logical requirement, that after death all creatures be raised to life, and that all people appear before Him who created them and who subjected the universe to them and blessed them with its bounties, so that they may answer for their whole life, accounting and reckoning may take place, reward and punishment be given, and the trial through action be completed.

The depiction of the signs of power begins thus: first, attention is drawn to the great natural scenes. One portion is given to the heavens, and one portion is given to the vast and extensive earth, and then the wonders of life and creation scattered upon this earth come into view.

After this, it is said with great astonishment: what, then, is the proof these people have for not believing in resurrection after death? These people, after such natural evidences and after the confrontation with signs and miracles, are in fact inviting the punishment of Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 13, verses 2–7 (part 1 of 2):

Verses 2 to 7

What the heavens are, and what people in different eras have understood their meaning to be, is a separate matter; but they are before our eyes. This is a great, unique and magnificent universe. Whenever anyone reflects on it and continues to acquire knowledge, its greatness only increases. Then, this entire system stands without any visible support, just as nothing on this earth stands without a support that can be seen. Without pillars [﻿...]

This is the first brushstroke in the portrayal of this entire universe, and for human intuition and perceptive faculty it is a first blow, especially when a person is contemplating this great universe and wonders who that mighty power is that created this great universe and has held it in place in this way. It can only be Allah.

People build a small structure on some corner of the earth, with or without pillars, and then they praise these structures: how great a building is this, how beautiful a building is this? Yet they overlook the heights and beauties that exist within this universe. Without pillars, the celestial bodies stand in their own places. The power that operates behind this universe, the majesty that lies hidden, and the beauty that this power has placed within it are all worth seeing.

This great universe that is within our sight, and that great universe which is still hidden from our sight, where is the capital of the universe?

﴿ثُمَّ اسْتَوَىٰ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ﴾ (13:2) "Then He established Himself above the Throne." If this universe is high, the Throne of Allah is higher; and if this universe is great, the Throne of Allah is greater. Every sense of istiwa' carries the meaning of expanse, majesty and firm establishment, and the Qur'an has used the word istawa only to convey to the limited human perceptive faculty, because human perception is limited and weak.

This is the second brushstroke of the wondrous pen of divine power. The first brushstroke concerned those heights that are visible to human beings, and this second brushstroke concerns those heights that lie beyond the range of our limited vision. Within the context of the discourse, both these pictures appear together. Now, descending from the general concept of height, the theme of the subjugation of the universe is taken up. We see the atmosphere in which Allah has subjected the sun and the moon, and we know about it. To the extent that we have been able to know about them, the greatness of this system grips the reach of thought, and invites reason to realize that these mighty forces are in the power of Allah the Mighty, before whom we shall have to present ourselves.

Then, within the scene that has been portrayed, there are countless contrasting scenes. On the one hand there are those heights of the universe that are visible, but opposite them are also those heights that are hidden from our sight. Then, on one hand there is the height of this universe, and opposite this height and greatness is the helplessness and subjugation of this great universe; there is the mutual contest of the sun and the moon, there is the contest of night and day, and there is the mutual contest of stars and planets.

Then, besides the heights and the subjugation of the universe, within it there is a distinguished aspect: the wisely ordering aspect of divine wisdom.

﴿كُلٌّ يَجْرِي لِأَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى﴾ (13:2) "Each runs for a term appointed." Their height and their movement are for an appointed term, and this term is determined within a fixed divine law. This term is fixed both in the daily course of the sun and the moon and in their circuit in orbit. At no place can they deviate from that appointed term, and there is also a set time when this entire system will be rolled up and this whole universe will be brought to an end.

﴿يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ (13:2) "He manages the affair." That is, the sun and the moon are moving precisely according to their times and up to their appointed term, and will continue to move; and the Divine Being who is causing these magnificent marvels to move in this vast atmosphere without any visible support has fixed a time for them, and they cannot in any way go beyond their appointed time, because that exalted Being is the Manager, and there is no doubt that He is Most Majestic.

One manifestation of Allah's managing majesty is that ﴿يُفَصِّلُ الْآيَاتِ﴾ (13:2) "He details the signs." He presents them in an organized, interconnected manner, and brings every thing at its appointed time, brings it in accordance with causes, and brings it with defined purposes. Why?

﴿لَعَلَّكُم بِلِقَاءِ رَبِّكُمْ تُوقِنُونَ﴾ (13:2) "So that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord." Because when a person sees that the signs of Allah are detailed and interconnected, and that cosmic signs also support them, these cosmic signs are those that Allah has placed in this universe from the time of its creation; and along with these natural proofs and indications, Allah also sent down scriptural signs and proofs and thus confirmed them. As a result of all these signs and proofs, a person inevitably reaches the conclusion that after this life there is another life, where human deeds will be assessed and people will be rewarded or punished for those deeds. These are the outcomes of Allah's creation whose manifestation is through the wisdom of creation.

Now this great line of the portrayal of the scenes of nature descends from the higher world to the lower world, and the lower world is portrayed thus:

﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي مَدَّ الْأَرْضَ ... يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾ (13:3) "And it is He who spread out the earth, placed in it firm mountains and rivers, made in it of every fruit two mates, and covers the night over the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect." In the portrayal of the earth, its first colour is that it has been spread out. It lies spread before our eyes, and it is wide in length and breadth. Although its true shape is round, along with being round it is extensive in length and breadth. This is the first colour of this portrayal. After this, towering mountains appear in the picture. After that, rivers are seen between the mountains. Thus the initial features of this earth are determined, which make this scene exceedingly harmonious.

For the determination of the general features of the earth, it is necessary that here the most fundamental and general phenomena be mentioned: the important principle of life within the earth, and the fundamental manifestation for sustaining that life, namely the division into female and male within plant and animal life. The existence of male and female in animal life is obvious, but the system of male and female within vegetable life is itself a principle for the establishment of life.

﴿مِن كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ جَعَلَ فِيهَا زَوْجَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ (13:3) "Of every fruit He made in it two mates." This is the first fundamental manifestation. And ﴿يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ﴾ (13:3) "He covers the night over the day." He has made pairs of all fruits. In one tree there are two kinds of organs. Some trees are female or male, and some are male. This is the characteristic that opens the way for human beings to point towards the secrets and mysteries of this universe. That is, the colours of night and day, and of male and female among animals, are evident; but in fruits, reproduction and propagation was a mystery.

The very scene of night and day, where night and day come one after another and cover each other, and their system is very strange and enchanting, is a subject of deep reflection. The arrival of night and the departure of day, the appearance of dawn and the dispersal of the darkness of night: this is an event with which we have become so familiar and accustomed, having seen night and day, that it has no effect on the screen of our feeling. Yet in their reality they are astonishing and amazing. If we cast our habit aside a little, and abandon our mental torpor, and look at this universe with poetic sensitivity, and do not consider this continuous movement of night and day to be a commonplace thing, then this system of the passage of days reveals a profound divine wisdom, and it becomes clear that within it the wondrous craftsmanship of the Creator of the universe is manifest.

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِّقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾ (13:3) "Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect." Before moving on from this scene, it is appropriate that we cast a glance at the contrasting matters presented in this scene. For example, on one side are lofty mountains standing firm, and on the other side are flowing streams and rivers. In all fruits there are male and female. There are night and day, facing each other; there is the earth that is spread out, and there is the sky that is at great heights; and both are important and mutually complementary points of this great universe. Both are parts of the great universe.

These were the general features and the broad outlines of this universe and of the heavens and the earth. Now let us look at the very fine lines and the manner of the earth.

﴿وَفِي الْأَرْضِ قِطَعٌ ... يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (13:4) "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of vines, and fields, and palm trees, some multiple and some single, all watered with one water; yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason."

These natural phenomena are such that most of us see them with our own eyes, yet no thought arises within us to find out their reality.

﴿وَفِي الْأَرْضِ قِطَعٌ مُّتَجَاوِرَاتٌ﴾ (13:4) "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts." The characteristics of these tracts are distinct. If these tracts were not of distinct characteristic and nature, they would not be called tracts but would be called a single tract. That is, among them some tracts are good and fertile, and some are barren and bare. Some are deserts without water or vegetation, and some are pure rocks. And within these again there are pieces of various degrees, of many kinds: some for towns and settlements, some for forests and greenery, and some are waterless and dead plains. Some are irrigated and some are rain-fed, and thus there are pieces of every kind which resemble one another and are also distinct from one another, and all of them are part of this earth.

These were the initial and general lines in the portrayal of the earth. After this, detailed colours are now filled into this picture and various particular things emerge: crops, the date palm and the vine. These plants: the vine is the representative of those plants that creep over the ground, on roofs and trees; the date palm is representative of those plants that take the form of tall trees; and the others, crops, flowers and grain, are representative of those that stand in intermediate form. By mentioning these three, the intention is to indicate three kinds of different scenes. Thus colours are filled into this picture, and sample representative plants are given within it.

These date palms are both single and multiple. That is, some have a single trunk, and some are multiple from one root, two or more. All are irrigated by one water, there is one soil, yet the fruits of all the trees are different and have different tastes.

﴿وَنُفَضِّلُ بَعْضَهَا عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ فِي الْأُكُلِ﴾ (13:4) "Yet We make some of them excel others in fruit." Of the various fruits and plants of one region we have tasted, the taste of each differs from the other. Has ever we reflected on the point to which the Qur'an directs the heart and mind of man? It is such points that show that the Qur'an is a modern book, because the Qur'an gives freshness to human sensation, intuition and consciousness regarding facts that have become commonplace, whether these scenes relate to the cosmos or to the human soul. These points are so numerous that if a person spent his whole life he could not encompass them, and nor will the points and wonders of the Qur'an come to an end in coming eras.

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِّقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (13:4) "Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason." Here it should be kept in mind that a new contrast is found again: two pieces of earth are opposite and of different kinds. Date palms too are opposite, single and multiple. Then the tastes of different fruits differ. And plants are also different: crops, trees and vines.

After this cursory glance at this wider universe, now a note of wonder is expressed about people who do not reflect upon the proofs and signs found in this universe and in the self and the horizons, and whose reason does not reach the conclusion that this great universe has a Creator, or that there exists a mighty power, dominion and wise ordering wisdom that is running it. Their intellects are then, as it were, afflicted with torpor. Their hearts are narrow, and the springs of their thinking have dried up. Is this situation not astonishing?

﴿وَإِن تَعْجَبْ فَعَجَبٌ ... خَالِدُونَ﴾ (13:5) "And if you are to wonder, then wondrous is their saying: 'When we have become dust, shall we indeed be created anew?' These are the ones who have disbelieved in their Lord. These are the ones with shackles upon their necks. They are the companions of the Fire, and they will abide therein forever." This is the astonishing matter, and one should be astonished at what these people say: that when we have become dust, we shall then be raised again?

Is there anything surprising in this? The One who created this vast universe and who sustains it with such marvelous order has the power to bring people back to life in a new form. Whoever considers this impossible is in fact denying their Creator and the Administrator of the universe. Such people have in fact imprisoned their intellect and do not make use of their reason. Therefore Allah will also punish them in a similar way, so that there will be great shackles around their necks. Since their action is such, that is, binding the intellect, the punishment is of the same kind, that is, great shackles placed around their necks. This is because they have rendered inoperative that distinctive human quality because of which a human being is honored above other animals. They have adopted backwardness in the world, so Allah has prescribed for them in the Hereafter a life that is even more backward than this worldly life, because these people, by suspending thought, understanding, perception and intuition, live here merely like animals.

These people wonder how Allah will raise them up as a new creation. But their very wonder is in fact astonishing. They demand that you bring the punishment upon them quickly, and it is also astonishing that instead of asking for guidance and seeking the mercy of Allah, they demand the punishment of Allah.

﴿They hasten you to evil before good﴾ (13:6). These people do not reflect upon this universe and upon the self and the horizons, although the signs of Allah are scattered throughout this entire universe, in the earth and in the heavens. Then, have these people not become an example and a lesson for those who were destroyed before them?

﴿And indeed, examples have already passed before them﴾ (13:6). And these people do not reflect upon those examples, although there was a lesson in them for them.

Indeed, Allah is very merciful to His servants. Even if they commit wrongdoing for a period, Allah always keeps open the door of His mercy so that they may enter it through the path of repentance. But He sends punishment only upon those who insist upon the descent of the punishment of Allah, who are surrounded by sins and are not prepared to enter through the open door of Allah.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is severe in penalty﴾ (13:6). Here in the context of the discourse, Allah's forgiveness has been placed before His punishment, whereas these people were hastening toward the demand for punishment and were refusing to accept guidance, so that it may be known how great is the good that Allah wills for people, while these people themselves desire a great evil for themselves. As a result of this situation, it appears that these people are blind in insight, blind in their hearts, and that they deserve the Fire of Hell because of their obstinacy.

After this, the discourse turns to the point that how strange is the attitude of these people: the countless proofs of creation scattered throughout this universe are not visible to them, yet these people demand one particular miracle. They demand only one miracle from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and their eyes are not upon the thousands of miracles of the universe.

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide﴾ (13:7). These people demand a miracle, whereas the occurrence of miracles is not in the hand of the Messenger, nor is it a personal attribute of his. Miracles are sent by Allah, and He sends them when Allah perceives the need for them. O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, you are only a warner, just as the station of the messengers before you was to be warners to their people. Allah has sent countless messengers for the guidance of countless nations. Therefore, the sending of miracles is the work of that Being who is the Administrator of this universe and of the servants.

Because when a person sees that the signs of Allah are detailed and interconnected, and that cosmic signs also support them, these cosmic signs are those that Allah has placed in this universe from the time of its creation; and along with these natural proofs and indications, Allah also sent down scriptural signs and proofs and thus confirmed them. As a result of all these signs and proofs, a person inevitably reaches the conclusion that after this life there is another life, where human deeds will be assessed and people will be rewarded or punished for those deeds. These are the outcomes of Allah's creation whose manifestation is through the wisdom of creation.

Now this great line of the portrayal of the scenes of nature descends from the higher world to the lower world, and the lower world is portrayed thus:

﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي مَدَّ الْأَرْضَ ... يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾ (13:3) "And it is He who spread out the earth, placed in it firm mountains and rivers, made in it of every fruit two mates, and covers the night over the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect." In the portrayal of the earth, its first colour is that it has been spread out. It lies spread before our eyes, and it is wide in length and breadth. Although its true shape is round, along with being round it is extensive in length and breadth. This is the first colour of this portrayal. After this, towering mountains appear in the picture. After that, rivers are seen between the mountains. Thus the initial features of this earth are determined, which make this scene exceedingly harmonious.

For the determination of the general features of the earth, it is necessary that here the most fundamental and general phenomena be mentioned: the important principle of life within the earth, and the fundamental manifestation for sustaining that life, namely the division into female and male within plant and animal life. The existence of male and female in animal life is obvious, but the system of male and female within vegetable life is itself a principle for the establishment of life.

﴿مِن كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ جَعَلَ فِيهَا زَوْجَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ (13:3) "Of every fruit He made in it two mates." This is the first fundamental manifestation. And ﴿يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ﴾ (13:3) "He covers the night over the day." He has made pairs of all fruits. In one tree there are two kinds of organs. Some trees are female or male, and some are male. This is the characteristic that opens the way for human beings to point towards the secrets and mysteries of this universe. That is, the colours of night and day, and of male and female among animals, are evident; but in fruits, reproduction and propagation was a mystery.

The very scene of night and day, where night and day come one after another and cover each other, and their system is very strange and enchanting, is a subject of deep reflection. The arrival of night and the departure of day, the appearance of dawn and the dispersal of the darkness of night: this is an event with which we have become so familiar and accustomed, having seen night and day, that it has no effect on the screen of our feeling. Yet in their reality they are astonishing and amazing. If we cast our habit aside a little, and abandon our mental torpor, and look at this universe with poetic sensitivity, and do not consider this continuous movement of night and day to be a commonplace thing, then this system of the passage of days reveals a profound divine wisdom, and it becomes clear that within it the wondrous craftsmanship of the Creator of the universe is manifest.

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِّقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾ (13:3) "Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect." Before moving on from this scene, it is appropriate that we cast a glance at the contrasting matters presented in this scene. For example, on one side are lofty mountains standing firm, and on the other side are flowing streams and rivers. In all fruits there are male and female. There are night and day, facing each other; there is the earth that is spread out, and there is the sky that is at great heights; and both are important and mutually complementary points of this great universe. Both are parts of the great universe.

These were the general features and the broad outlines of this universe and of the heavens and the earth. Now let us look at the very fine lines and the manner of the earth.

﴿وَفِي الْأَرْضِ قِطَعٌ ... يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (13:4) "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of vines, and fields, and palm trees, some multiple and some single, all watered with one water; yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason."

These natural phenomena are such that most of us see them with our own eyes, yet no thought arises within us to find out their reality.

﴿وَفِي الْأَرْضِ قِطَعٌ مُّتَجَاوِرَاتٌ﴾ (13:4) "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts." The characteristics of these tracts are distinct. If these tracts were not of distinct characteristic and nature, they would not be called tracts but would be called a single tract. That is, among them some tracts are good and fertile, and some are barren and bare. Some are deserts without water or vegetation, and some are pure rocks. And within these again there are pieces of various degrees, of many kinds: some for towns and settlements, some for forests and greenery, and some are waterless and dead plains. Some are irrigated and some are rain-fed, and thus there are pieces of every kind which resemble one another and are also distinct from one another, and all of them are part of this earth.

These were the initial and general lines in the portrayal of the earth. After this, detailed colours are now filled into this picture and various particular things emerge: crops, the date palm and the vine. These plants: the vine is the representative of those plants that creep over the ground, on roofs and trees; the date palm is representative of those plants that take the form of tall trees; and the others, crops, flowers and grain, are representative of those that stand in intermediate form. By mentioning these three, the intention is to indicate three kinds of different scenes. Thus colours are filled into this picture, and sample representative plants are given within it.

These date palms are both single and multiple. That is, some have a single trunk, and some are multiple from one root, two or more. All are irrigated by one water, there is one soil, yet the fruits of all the trees are different and have different tastes.

Of the various fruits and plants of one region we have tasted, the taste of each differs from the other. Has ever we reflected on the point to which the Qur'an directs the heart and mind of man? It is such points that show that the Qur'an is a modern book, because the Qur'an gives freshness to human sensation, intuition and consciousness regarding facts that have become commonplace, whether these scenes relate to the cosmos or to the human soul. These points are so numerous that if a person spent his whole life he could not encompass them, and nor will the points and wonders of the Qur'an come to an end in coming eras.

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِّقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (13:4) "Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason." Here it should be kept in mind that a new contrast is found again: two pieces of earth are opposite and of different kinds. Date palms too are opposite, single and multiple. Then the tastes of different fruits differ. And plants are also different: crops, trees and vines.

After this cursory glance at this wider universe, now a note of wonder is expressed about people who do not reflect upon the proofs and signs found in this universe and in the self and the horizons, and whose reason does not reach the conclusion that this great universe has a Creator, or that there exists a mighty power, dominion and wise ordering wisdom that is running it. Their intellects are then, as it were, afflicted with torpor. Their hearts are narrow, and the springs of their thinking have dried up. Is this situation not astonishing?

﴿وَإِن تَعْجَبْ فَعَجَبٌ ... خَالِدُونَ﴾ (13:5) "And if you are to wonder, then wondrous is their saying: 'When we have become dust, shall we indeed be created anew?' These are the ones who have disbelieved in their Lord. These are the ones with shackles upon their necks. They are the companions of the Fire, and they will abide therein forever." This is the astonishing matter, and one should be astonished at what these people say: that when we have become dust, we shall then be raised again?

Whoever considers this impossible is in fact denying their Creator and the Administrator of the universe. Such people have in fact imprisoned their intellect and do not make use of their reason. Therefore Allah will also punish them in a similar way, so that there will be great shackles around their necks. Since their action is such, that is, binding the intellect, the punishment is of the same kind, that is, great shackles placed around their necks. This is because they have rendered inoperative that distinctive human quality because of which a human being is honored above other animals. They have adopted backwardness in the world, so Allah has prescribed for them in the Hereafter a life that is even more backward than this worldly life, because these people, by suspending thought, understanding, perception and intuition, live here merely like animals.

These people wonder how Allah will raise them up as a new creation. But their very wonder is in fact astonishing. They demand that you bring the punishment upon them quickly, and it is also astonishing that instead of asking for guidance and seeking the mercy of Allah, they demand the punishment of Allah.

﴿They hasten you to evil before good﴾ (13:6). These people do not reflect upon this universe and upon the self and the horizons, although the signs of Allah are scattered throughout this entire universe, in the earth and in the heavens. Then, have these people not become an example and a lesson for those who were destroyed before them?

﴿And indeed, examples have already passed before them﴾ (13:6). And these people do not reflect upon those examples, although there was a lesson in them for them.

Indeed, Allah is very merciful to His servants. Even if they commit wrongdoing for a period, Allah always keeps open the door of His mercy so that they may enter it through the path of repentance. But He sends punishment only upon those who insist upon the descent of the punishment of Allah, who are surrounded by sins and are not prepared to enter through the open door of Allah.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is severe in penalty﴾ (13:6). Here in the context of the discourse, Allah's forgiveness has been placed before His punishment, whereas these people were hastening toward the demand for punishment and were refusing to accept guidance, so that it may be known how great is the good that Allah wills for people, while these people themselves desire a great evil for themselves. As a result of this situation, it appears that these people are blind in insight, blind in their hearts, and that they deserve the Fire of Hell because of their obstinacy.

After this, the discourse turns to the point that how strange is the attitude of these people: the countless proofs of creation scattered throughout this universe are not visible to them, yet these people demand one particular miracle. They demand only one miracle from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and their eyes are not upon the thousands of miracles of the universe.

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide﴾ (13:7). These people demand a miracle, whereas the occurrence of miracles is not in the hand of the Messenger, nor is it a personal attribute of his. Miracles are sent by Allah, and He sends them when Allah perceives the need for them. O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, you are only a warner, just as the station of the messengers before you was to be warners to their people. Allah has sent countless messengers for the guidance of countless nations. Therefore, the sending of miracles is the work of that Being who is the Administrator of this universe and of the servants.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 13, verses 8–11:

This was a passing glance at the horizons of the universe. Comments were made on it; now you will be taken into certain particular valleys of the universe. For example, reflection on the human self (nafs), human consciousness and perception, human life on this earth, and other living things.

Verses 8 to 11

When these scenes are presented in depicting human life, human sense and consciousness are struck dumb, especially by the melodious style of the Qur'an. Seeing the wonders of God's knowledge and God's wisdoms, a person is left astonished. The knowledge that has been revealed to man about the embryo, then the secrets that every person has hidden in his breast, the movements and exertions of a person at night, the activities of people done secretly and the struggles of people openly during the day, God knows all these matters well, and God's agents also record all these activities. This astonishment of man is in fact due to the fear of God, as a result of which man seeks refuge in God. He seeks refuge in the very refuge of God. A believer knows well and believes that God's knowledge encompasses all things, but acknowledging in principle the inclusion and extent of God's knowledge is one thing, and the effect of the way the Qur'an mentions certain particulars here, with its striking impact, is another.

Merely stating an abstract rule is one thing, and studying a exemplary particular under a rule is another. Here God, exalted is He, mentions certain particulars, sensitive particulars.

﴿God knows what every female carries...﴾ (13:8) "God knows what every female carries in her womb, and what the wombs lack or exceed, He is aware of it. Everything has a measure with Him."

From the veil of imagination, every pregnant female comes to mind, every pregnant female in the whole universe in the broad sense: every pregnant female in cities and villages, in settlements and mountains, in forests and rivers, in houses and caves. Whatever is being created, growing or diminishing in the womb of every female, every drop of blood that is growing or diminishing, God knows all of it.

This is a particular example, and it is not an abstract rule that God knows everything and that is all; rather, it is a matter of a specific branch of knowledge.

﴿Whether one of you speaks secretly or openly...﴾ (13:10–11) "Whether one of you speaks in a low voice or loudly, and whether one is hidden in the darkness of the night or walking in the light of day, they are all alike to Him. For every person there are successive watchers before and behind him, who guard him by the command of God."

When one thinks of whisperers on the human thought, of one who speaks aloud, of those who walk in darkness and those who move in daylight, and then of this entire universe, and then of the thought that God's knowledge pursues all of them and His agents are also writing, and sending reports at both ends of the night. Then also consider the manner of expression of these particulars of divine knowledge:

﴿God knows what every female carries...﴾ (13:8) When God said that He knows the increase and decrease in the womb, at the end He said that with God everything has a measure. Bringing the word "measure" alongside deficiency and excess creates a balance. Moreover, it is connected to the verse before it, in which it is mentioned that people wonder how, after death and becoming dust, they will rise again in a new creation. Also, in subject and outward form, it resembles the theme about rain, where rain falls and valleys flow with water according to their measure. In all matters, measure is observed. Increase, decrease and measure are the special point of this surah.

﴿He knows the unseen and the visible, the Great, the Most High﴾ (13:9) "He is the knower of the hidden and the manifest; He is the Great, the Exalted, who remains above in every state." The words "kabir" (great) and "muta'al" (exalted) both leave a particular impression on the sensibility; I describe this as a reflection (pur-tau). It is difficult to express it with any other word. That is, every creature has some defect within it which makes it small. We cannot call any of God's creatures "great," or any other matter "great." As soon as God is mentioned, all other matters become small. Likewise, our thinking about the word "muta'al" is limited. No commentator has said anything about the scope of the morality of "al-Kabir al-Muta'al."

﴿Whether one of you speaks secretly or openly...﴾ (13:10) "Whether one of you speaks loudly or softly, and whether one is hidden in the darkness of night or walking in the light of day, they are alike to Him." The contrast in the expression is clear. The word "sarib" deserves reflection. The word "sarib" itself sheds light on its meaning. Its meaning is concealment and hiddenness, or nearly so. The meaning of "sarib" is one who walks in the light, that is, God knows even hidden things. The fetus that is hidden, secrets that are concealed, the person who walks in the darkness of night, then God's agents who are not visible: "sarib" is a word opposite to "khafi" (hidden), but within it too there is a reflection of gentleness, subtlety and concealment.

﴿For him there are successive watchers before and behind him...﴾ (13:11) "For every person there are watchers before and behind him, appointed for him, who guard him by the command of God." The angels appointed for the protection of human beings protect every comer and goer, and save humans from every whisper and every disturbance. They act according to God's commands. Here no definition or detail of these watchers is given. Only this description is given here: "min amri Allah," those who act by God's command. We too leave them in general terms here: what they are, what their attributes are, how they carry out this watch, where they are located. Since God has kept this matter hidden, and it is from this concealment that the fear that is desired here is produced, we are content with what the Qur'an has said. And this concealment and generality is not accidental or purposeless. For those who have any understanding of the style of expression of the Holy Qur'an, it is difficult to dispel an atmosphere that the Qur'an creates, because giving details would destroy that impression.

﴿Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people...﴾ (13:11) "Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves." God watches over people through His agents, so that they see what changes people bring about within themselves and what efforts they make to change their circumstances. For God, the exalted, does not change the state of a people in progress or decline, in honour or disgrace, in height or fall, until people change their own thinking, their consciousness, their deeds and their activities. Thus God also brings about changes in people's conditions according to their thoughts and their thinking and actions, even though God already knows what they will do and what they will not do. The practical results emerge according to people's thought and action. Yes, these results come about in practice in the period determined along with people's lives.

This is the truth, as a result of which God, exalted is He, has placed a very great responsibility upon humanity. This was the demand of God's will, and according to it the sunnah of God continues in force, that the conditions of people depend on people changing. The divine sunnah is established on their conduct and their way of thinking. This is a clear text, so there is no room for interpretation or distortion in it. Through the determination of this divine sunnah, God has made the human being most honoured, in that the divine sunnah is formed by the action of man himself.

After the establishment of this divine sunnah, the context of the speech makes clear what the sunnah is when God brings a people to destruction. It too is the same: when people bring about evil change within themselves, then the divine sunnah also shows them evil days.

﴿And when God intends to bring calamity upon a people, there is no turning it back, and they have no protector besides Him﴾ (13:11).

Here the context describes this aspect of decline in this way, because the subject and theme here is such that people are more eager for evil than for good. Whereas God has told them that He thinks of their forgiveness before punishment. The purpose is to show how heedless these people have become. Therefore their evil end is mentioned here so that they may fear and come to their senses, because God's decisions are firm, and when the decree of your destruction has come, then no one will be your supporter or helper.

Then also consider the manner of expression of these particulars of divine knowledge:

﴿God knows what every female carries...﴾ (13:8) When God said that He knows the increase and decrease in the womb, at the end He said that with God everything has a measure. Bringing the word "measure" alongside deficiency and excess creates a balance. Moreover, it is connected to the verse before it, in which it is mentioned that people wonder how, after death and becoming dust, they will rise again in a new creation. Also, in subject and outward form, it resembles the theme about rain, where rain falls and valleys flow with water according to their measure. In all matters, measure is observed. Increase, decrease and measure are the special point of this surah.

﴿He knows the unseen and the visible, the Great, the Most High﴾ (13:9) "He is the knower of the hidden and the manifest; He is the Great, the Exalted, who remains above in every state." The words "kabir" (great) and "muta'al" (exalted) both leave a particular impression on the sensibility; I describe this as a reflection (pur-tau). It is difficult to express it with any other word. That is, every creature has some defect within it which makes it small. We cannot call any of God's creatures "great," or any other matter "great." As soon as God is mentioned, all other matters become small. Likewise, our thinking about the word "muta'al" is limited. No commentator has said anything about the scope of the morality of "al-Kabir al-Muta'al."

﴿Whether one of you speaks secretly or openly...﴾ (13:10) "Whether one of you speaks loudly or softly, and whether one is hidden in the darkness of night or walking in the light of day, they are alike to Him." The contrast in the expression is clear. The word "sarib" deserves reflection. The word "sarib" itself sheds light on its meaning. Its meaning is concealment and hiddenness, or nearly so. The meaning of "sarib" is one who walks in the light, that is, God knows even hidden things. For God, the exalted, does not change the state of a people in progress or decline, in honour or disgrace, in height or fall, until people change their own thinking, their consciousness, their deeds and their activities. Thus God also brings about changes in people's conditions according to their thoughts and their thinking and actions, even though God already knows what they will do and what they will not do. The practical results emerge according to people's thought and action. Yes, these results come about in practice in the period determined along with people's lives.

This is the truth, as a result of which God, exalted is He, has placed a very great responsibility upon humanity. This was the demand of God's will, and according to it the sunnah of God continues in force, that the conditions of people depend on people changing. The divine sunnah is established on their conduct and their way of thinking. This is a clear text, so there is no room for interpretation or distortion in it. Through the determination of this divine sunnah, God has made the human being most honoured, in that the divine sunnah is formed by the action of man himself.

After the establishment of this divine sunnah, the context of the speech makes clear what the sunnah is when God brings a people to destruction. It too is the same: when people bring about evil change within themselves, then the divine sunnah also shows them evil days.

Here the context describes this aspect of decline in this way, because the subject and theme here is such that people are more eager for evil than for good. Whereas God has told them that He thinks of their forgiveness before punishment. The purpose is to show how heedless these people have become. Therefore their evil end is mentioned here so that they may fear and come to their senses, because God's decisions are firm, and when the decree of your destruction has come, then no one will be your supporter or helper.

Verses 12 to 16

Lightning, thunder and clouds are common scenes. Likewise, at times lightning also strikes from these scenes. These are scenes that affect every human being, whether or not one is acquainted with their natural reality. Here the Qur'an, while presenting them, also mentions along with them the angels, glorification (tasbih), prostration (sujud), fear, desire, and the shadow of these sights, and it is also mentioned what true supplication is and what false and unjust supplication is. Among these scenes, the figure of another person is presented who wishes to drink water but does not stretch out his hand toward it; rather, with his hand open and his mouth open, he wishes that the water would fall into his mouth of its own accord, while it is not going to fall, not even a drop.

All these scenes, examples and objects are not gathered in this verse merely by chance and without purpose; all of these things are in fact related to the subject under discussion. Rather, these scenes have been brought to frighten people, to give hope, ... to instill both desire and fear, and to make people aware of the hopes of gain and loss, and to negate the power of the other partners that people have set up alongside Allah.

"He it is who shows you the lightning, [causing] fear and hope" (13:12). Allah is the One who shows you these natural phenomena. These are the natural and meteorological manifestations of this universe which He created, and He created this universe in this particular manner and placed these properties within these things. The lightning which Allah shows you operates according to His law of nature. You are also frightened by it, because its very nature is such that it shakes the nerves. Sometimes this lightning also strikes as a bolt and causes destruction in a terrifying form, as you must have experienced many times ... Then after this flash and lightning you also become hopeful of the mercy of rain, because after this flash and thunder, at times heavy rain falls and the dead earth comes to life.

"And He produces the heavy clouds" (13:12). He is also the One who creates the clouds. Sahab (السحاب) is the collective noun whose singular is sahabah, meaning a single piece of cloud. Thiqal refers to clouds that are heavy because of the rain. These clouds come into being according to the natural order that Allah has created and they pour down heavy rains. If Allah had not established the laws of nature in this way, there would be neither clouds nor such rains. Saying how clouds come into being and how rains fall, knowing their scientific and empirical description, does not diminish their beauty and enchanting quality, nor does it alter the meaning that the Qur'an has derived. For all these works and processes take place solely according to the cosmic system created by Allah; no human craftsmanship has any part in them, and humans have no role or action in this entire system. The natural and physical principles by which this universe runs were neither created by the universe itself nor did they start moving on their own; whatever runs in it runs by virtue of an absolute Creator.

Among the scenes of thunder, wind and rain there is a particular scene: this long and crashing sound. This too is a manifestation of the laws of nature of this earth and is the craftsmanship of Allah. Whatever its scientific analysis may be, who can deny that it is a part of Allah's creation? It glorifies Allah in the sense that it moves along the law of nature according to which Allah has made this system, just as whenever one sees a beautifully made thing, praise and commendation of its maker spontaneously arise, and on seeing the traces, beauty and utility of his handiwork, everyone offers praise. In the same way, upon seeing the perfections and astonishing benefits found within this universe, the glorification of Allah spontaneously comes to the tongue. This meaning of tasbih may also be valid, and thunder itself is calling out. In any case, we have not yet understood the glorification of these things, and even without understanding it we believe in these realities. Even about ourselves we still know little. It may be that after some time we will also find out how these things glorify.

Here the Qur'an has adopted a manner of expression regarding thunder as though thunder were a living creature that is glorifying. It is the particular style of the Qur'an that it adorns the scenes of divine power with signs of life, although these scenes of power are silent; and this is because in this whole scene all the other scenes are alive, as I have given details in my book at-Tasweer al-Fanni fil-Quran. In this scene, since there are scenes of living things, for example glorifying, calling upon Allah, calling upon partners, and the scene of a man standing before water with his hands outstretched, expecting it to fall into his mouth of its own accord while it is not going to fall, then in scenes where on one side there is calling, servitude and movement, the thunder too has been imagined as living, and glorification and supplication have been attributed to it.

Now this scene is made even more frightening: fear, supplication, lightning and thunder, heavy clouds, and rain showers; now lightning is also seen striking, and upon some helpless one lightning falls. The way this lightning strikes is part of the natural order of this universe. At times this lightning strikes a person whom Allah does not wish to give further respite, because Allah alone knows that it is not appropriate to give such people more time; therefore some people are destroyed by this lightning.

And the astonishing thing is that in this atmosphere of thunder and lightning, storm, clouds and rain, and with the glorification by thunder and lightning and the expression of obedience by the angels in a state of fear, and even in the state of the peak of these wrathful manifestations of Allah's power, there are some people who express doubts about the Divine Being and engage in disputes and debates about Allah. Yet the manifestations of Allah's power, indeed these terrifying manifestations, they are seeing with their own eyes.

"Yet they dispute about Allah, while He is mighty in strength" (13:13). There are some people who speak about the Divine Being, but in this awe-inspiring atmosphere, amid weeping and wailing, thunder and lightning, roaring and crashing, and this tumultuous environment in which all things point to the existence of the Divine, the voices of these few people are drowned out. For all the notable scenes of this universe are a clear proof of Allah's oneness and of Allah's glorification and declaration of His unity; then, among the angels there are some who tremble constantly out of fear of Allah. Therefore, in the presence of these scenes, and the fear of these angels, and the fear of all humans, the words of those who speak about Allah are rare and out of place.

These people speak about Allah, for instance that they associate others with Allah, whereas the truth will be called upon, and the one who calls upon falsehood will call in vain.

"To Him is the true call; and those they call upon besides Him respond to them not at all, except as one who stretches his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is not but in error" (13:14). This scene is also an eloquent scene, dynamic and meaningful. The truth is that there is one true call, and it alone deserves it, and it is realistic; and whatever other calls there are, they are false, futile and misguided. Do you not reflect that among those who leave Allah and call upon others, one is like a man who is thirsty and weakened by thirst; he has spread out his arms, opened his hands, his mouth is open and he keeps calling constantly upon someone, upon the water before him: "O water, come into my mouth and fall!" But it is not going to fall. This person becomes exhausted and worn out in this calling and struggle, and his purpose is not fulfilled. This is the meaning of this verse.

"And it is not but as one who stretches his hands..." (13:14), "...but it does not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is not but in error." This example is given in an atmosphere in which a man parched with thirst cannot obtain even a drop of water. In such an atmosphere, in which on all sides there is a storm of lightning, wind and rain, and all these frightening scenes move according to Allah's law of nature.

At the time when these unsuccessful and misguided people call upon other deities besides Allah, hope for things other than Allah, and stand with supplicating hands before other than Allah, this entire universe and everything in it prostrate before Allah; all these people and all this creation are under the command of Allah and bound in the law of His power, moving according to the sunnah of Allah. Among this creation, the believer obeys with joy and willingness, and the disbelievers also obey unwillingly, because no thing can escape the will of Allah, nor can anything leave the divine order.

"And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows [too] in the mornings and evenings" (13:15). For this atmosphere is indeed the atmosphere of worship, servitude and supplication. In the context of the discourse, the Qur'an expresses carrying out Allah's commands with the word 'ibadah (worship), because in prostration a person adopts the utmost degree of humility and obedience. Along with this, mention is also made of the creation of the heavens and the earth, and even the shadows of all things in this universe are described as obedient to Allah, since these shadows also bow before Allah. As if they worship and serve Allah, because these shadows cannot deviate even a hair's breadth from divine obedience, and they are subject to the law of nature in the same way that a person who prostrates before Allah is subject. This is both an illustration and a reality, since a shadow is dependent on the rays of the sun. This illustration also affects the atmosphere of this scene, although there are two kinds of prostration: the prostration of individuals and the prostration of shadows. And this whole universe is also obedient to Allah, whether it submits by the path of faith or by non-faith, that is, through the law of nature. The entire universe is in any case prostrate. And these wretched polytheists are such that even in these circumstances they call upon other than Allah.

In this strange and wondrous scene and this impressive atmosphere, they are now questioned; questions are asked whose answer is nothing but "Yes," and thus they are made to be laughed at.

"Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah. Say: Have you then taken protectors other than Him who do not possess for themselves any benefit or harm?... Say: Is the blind equal to the seeing, or is darkness equal to light? Or have they attributed to Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed similar to them? Say: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer" (13:16). Ask them, while the reality is that whatever is in the heavens and the earths is derived from Allah's will and Allah's power. It is bound by Allah's power, whether it is pleased or not. This question, "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?", is not asked so that they may give an answer; the answer has already come within the context of the discourse. It is asked so that they may acknowledge it with their own tongues. The answer is indeed "Allah." Then the second question: do those whom you call upon possess power over their own benefit and harm? This question is also asked merely to rebuke them and to humiliate them. Keep asking, while this matter is perfectly clear; the distinction between truth and falsehood has already been made, to such an extent that it is like the difference between the blind and the one who has sight, or the difference between light and darkness. The reference to the blind and the seeing points to the fact that a believer is one who sees, and a disbeliever is one who is blind, because blindness is precisely what prevents a person from seeing the truth, although this truth is both manifest and hidden, and its signs can be perceived in the heavens and the earth. The mention of darkness and light also alludes to the conditions of those who deny and the conditions of the believers. Darkness becomes an obstacle in the path of seeing, and their condition is that veils stand between them and the truth.

The important question is: have those entities that these people associate with Allah created any creation as Allah has created creations? In this way they came to suspect that perhaps these too share in the act of creating, or they came to suspect which creation belongs to Allah and which creation belongs to those entities. Thus these wretched people are excused, and thus it is possible for them to commit this error of associating others with Allah in His essence and attributes. For in this supposition these entities would share in the attribute of creation; but if no creation belongs to anyone else at all, then what sense does partnership make?

This is a mockery of the people who claim that Allah alone, without partner, is the Creator, and yet they also ascribe partners to Allah. Yet the partners they ascribe, by their own admission, are not creators at all; they are themselves creatures. Nevertheless, they still regard them as deities and worship them. This is a most base specimen of thought, reflection, reason and insight.

And after this contemptuous mockery, a conclusion is drawn to which there is no room for argument or dispute.

﴿Say: Allah is the Creator of everything, and He is the One, the Irresistible.﴾ (13:16) That is, He is the One and Unique in creation, and He is the One and Unique in dominance and compulsion. Qahhar means the supreme, utterly dominant ruler. The doctrine of Tawhid and the refutation of shirk are encompassed here in such a way that all things in the heavens and the earth prostrate before Allah alone, whether a thing prostrates willingly (as man does) or under compulsion. At the end of this lesson, by mentioning Allah's Qahhariyyah, the issue of Tawhid is stated thus: Allah is a Ruler who is extremely dominant and has a firm grasp. All things of the heavens and the earth are obedient to Him, just as thunder, lightning and the crash are all glorifying Him. In such circumstances, only a blind or stone-hearted person would fail to feel the fear of Allah, and the destiny of such a person is nothing but destruction and ruin.

Before we conclude our discussion of this lesson, it is necessary that we reflect on certain opposing matters with regard to the manner of expression. For instance, within the thunder, the lightning and the heavy clouds there is mention of fear and hope, which are opposites. The clouds are mentioned with "thiqal" (heaviness), and because of their heaviness they move at a slow pace, whereas the flash and lightning are extremely swift. These two meanings are also mutually opposed and contrary. The glorification of thunder is accompanied by praise of Allah, while the glorification of the angels is accompanied by fear. These two are also opposing meanings. The call to truth and the call to falsehood are two opposing aims. The earth and the heavens are also mutually opposed; prostration by pleasure and prostration by compulsion, "taw'an wa karhan," are also opposing meanings. Individuals and their shadows, morning and evening, the blind and the seeing, darkness and light, the true Creator and the helpless partners, the one who holds the power of benefit and harm and their partners who own nothing. Thus, through mention of mutually contrary and opposing matters throughout this entire lesson, truth and falsehood have been explained. This is a most beautiful manner of expression, and it is indeed with a wondrous harmony.

There is a call to truth which always remains on the earth, and there is a call to falsehood which goes in the direction the wind blows. There is a goodness which is dignified and stays firmly established, and there is an evil and wrongdoing which appears to flourish. What is being presented here is the might of the One, the Irresistible Allah. This example is also of the same kind as those scenes of divine power which are the specific subject of this lesson.

This example is given in an atmosphere in which a man parched with thirst cannot obtain even a drop of water. In such an atmosphere, in which on all sides there is a storm of lightning, wind and rain, and all these frightening scenes move according to Allah's law of nature.

Among this creation, the believer obeys with joy and willingness, and the disbelievers also obey unwillingly, because no thing can escape the will of Allah, nor can anything leave the divine order.

This is both an illustration and a reality, since a shadow is dependent on the rays of the sun. This illustration also affects the atmosphere of this scene, although there are two kinds of prostration: the prostration of individuals and the prostration of shadows. And this whole universe is also obedient to Allah, whether it submits by the path of faith or by non-faith, that is, through the law of nature. The entire universe is in any case prostrate. In this strange and wondrous scene and this impressive atmosphere, they are now questioned; questions are asked whose answer is nothing but "Yes," and thus they are made to be laughed at.

This question is also asked merely to rebuke them and to humiliate them. The mention of darkness and light also alludes to the conditions of those who deny and the conditions of the believers. Darkness becomes an obstacle in the path of seeing, and their condition is that veils stand between them and the truth.

This is a most base specimen of thought, reflection, reason and insight.

And after this contemptuous mockery, a conclusion is drawn to which there is no room for argument or dispute.

In such circumstances, only a blind or stone-hearted person would fail to feel the fear of Allah, and the destiny of such a person is nothing but destruction and ruin.

These two meanings are also mutually opposed and contrary. The glorification of thunder is accompanied by praise of Allah, while the glorification of the angels is accompanied by fear. These two are also opposing meanings. The call to truth and the call to falsehood are two opposing aims. Individuals and their shadows, morning and evening, the blind and the seeing, darkness and light, the true Creator and the helpless partners, the one who holds the power of benefit and harm and their partners who own nothing. Thus, through mention of mutually contrary and opposing matters throughout this entire lesson, truth and falsehood have been explained. This is a most beautiful manner of expression, and it is indeed with a wondrous harmony.

Now let us move a little further. Allah presents another example of truth and falsehood. There is a call to truth which always remains on the earth, and there is a call to falsehood which goes in the direction the wind blows. There is a goodness which is dignified and stays firmly established, and there is an evil and wrongdoing which appears to flourish. What is being presented here is the might of the One, the Irresistible Allah. This example is also of the same kind as those scenes of divine power which are the specific subject of this lesson.

Now the section proceeds into a different valley. This valley too is connected to and integrated with the one we have just been traversing. It is the valley where natural scenes and the consciousness of the human self meet. In this valley, the natural phenomena, their reflection, and their effects come together in the picture of human consciousness. Fear, dread, struggle, hope and apprehension are intertwined, and human consciousness takes on various impressions in this valley.

Verses 12 to 16

These are scenes that affect every human being, whether or not one is acquainted with their natural reality. These are the natural and meteorological manifestations of this universe which He created, and He created this universe in this particular manner and placed these properties within these things. The lightning which Allah shows you operates according to His law of nature. You are also frightened by it, because its very nature is such that it shakes the nerves. Sometimes this lightning also strikes as a bolt and causes destruction in a terrifying form, as you must have experienced many times ... Then after this flash and lightning you also become hopeful of the mercy of rain, because after this flash and thunder, at times heavy rain falls and the dead earth comes to life.

Thiqal refers to clouds that are heavy because of the rain. These clouds come into being according to the natural order that Allah has created and they pour down heavy rains. If Allah had not established the laws of nature in this way, there would be neither clouds nor such rains. Saying how clouds come into being and how rains fall, knowing their scientific and empirical description, does not diminish their beauty and enchanting quality, nor does it alter the meaning that the Qur'an has derived. For all these works and processes take place solely according to the cosmic system created by Allah; no human craftsmanship has any part in them, and humans have no role or action in this entire system. The natural and physical principles by which this universe runs were neither created by the universe itself nor did they start moving on their own; whatever runs in it runs by virtue of an absolute Creator.

Among the scenes of thunder, wind and rain there is a particular scene: this long and crashing sound. This too is a manifestation of the laws of nature of this earth and is the craftsmanship of Allah. Whatever its scientific analysis may be, who can deny that it is a part of Allah's creation? It glorifies Allah in the sense that it moves along the law of nature according to which Allah has made this system, just as whenever one sees a beautifully made thing, praise and commendation of its maker spontaneously arise, and on seeing the traces, beauty and utility of his handiwork, everyone offers praise. In the same way, upon seeing the perfections and astonishing benefits found within this universe, the glorification of Allah spontaneously comes to the tongue. This meaning of tasbih may also be valid, and thunder itself is calling out. In any case, we have not yet understood the glorification of these things, and even without understanding it we believe in these realities. Even about ourselves we still know little. It may be that after some time we will also find out how these things glorify.
